The micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG), also called a voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG), is a fluoroscopic contrast study of the bladder and urethra. It is predominantly a paediatric investigation. The bladder is catheterised and filled with water-soluble contrast, then imaged both during filling and — crucially — during micturition, when the catheter is removed and the child voids. This voiding phase is what reveals vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and demonstrates the urethra, most importantly to exclude posterior urethral valves in boys.

1Indications — mostly paediatric

MCUG is requested to answer specific structural and functional questions about the lower urinary tract:

Vesicoureteric reflux — after atypical/recurrent UTI or antenatal hydronephrosis.
Posterior urethral valves — suspected bladder outlet obstruction in a neonatal/infant boy.
Bladder & urethral anatomy — diverticula, ureterocele, duplex systems, trauma.
Neuropathic bladder — e.g. spinal dysraphism, to assess bladder configuration and reflux.
Antenatal hydronephrosis + UTI in an infant→MCUG to look for reflux and (in boys) valves
2Technique — filling then voiding

An aseptic urethral catheter is passed and the bladder drained. It is then filled with iodinated water-soluble contrast under gravity while imaging with intermittent fluoroscopy. Barium is never used in the urinary tract. Images are taken:

During filling — bladder outline, capacity, wall (trabeculation, diverticula).
During micturition — the catheter is removed and the child voids; this is the key phase for detecting reflux (raised intravesical pressure) and imaging the urethra.
🎓 The voiding phase is non-negotiable — reflux and posterior urethral valves are frequently only demonstrated at the pressures generated during micturition, not during passive filling.
3What you assess
Bladder outline — shape, capacity, wall thickness/trabeculation, diverticula, ureterocele.
Ureteric reflux — presence, unilateral/bilateral, and graded severity.
Urethra during voiding — calibre and any obstruction (posterior urethral valves in boys).
4Key findings & signs

Vesicoureteric reflux is graded I–V (International Reflux Study System):

Grade I — reflux into a non-dilated ureter only.
Grade II — reflux up to the renal pelvis/calyces, no dilatation.
Grade III — mild–moderate dilatation of ureter and pelvicalyceal system; calyces mildly blunted.
Grade IV — moderate dilatation and tortuosity; calyces blunted/rounded.
Grade V — gross dilatation and tortuosity of the ureter with clubbed calyces; papillary impressions lost.
🔑Posterior urethral valves
Boys only. Dilated posterior urethra above the obstruction with an abrupt calibre change — the ‘keyhole’ sign. Thick-walled, trabeculated bladder. Important surgical cause of outlet obstruction in neonatal boys.
💧Vesicoureteric reflux
Retrograde contrast from bladder into ureter ± collecting system during filling or voiding; graded I–V. Risk of pyelonephritis and renal scarring.
🫧Bladder diverticulum
Contrast-filled outpouching through the bladder wall; may be congenital (e.g. para-ureteric Hutch diverticulum) or from chronic obstruction.
🎈Ureterocele
Cystic dilatation of the distal ureter within the bladder; seen as a rounded filling defect, classically at the lower-pole moiety insertion of a duplex system.
🎓 MCUG shows anatomy and reflux, but not renal function or scarring. Pair with a DMSA scan to look for cortical scarring and a MAG3 renogram to assess differential function and drainage.
🚩 Safety & consent: catheterisation carries an infection risk — cover with prophylactic antibiotics and use strict asepsis. The study is distressing for children (catheter + voiding on the table), so needs a calm, child-friendly environment. It delivers gonadal radiation to children, so must be justified; direct radionuclide cystography is a lower-dose alternative for follow-up of known reflux. Beware iodinated contrast reactions. Parental (proxy) consent is required.

The retrograde urethrogram (RUG) and the cystogram are paired fluoroscopic contrast studies of the lower urinary tract. The RUG opacifies the urethra from the meatus upwards and is the first-line test for suspected urethral injury; the cystogram fills and then drains the bladder to detect rupture, leak or fistula. The single most important rule: if urethral injury is suspected, do the retrograde urethrogram before any attempt at catheterisation.

🚩 Blood at the urethral meatus, a high-riding or non-palpable prostate, perineal/scrotal haematoma, or inability to void after pelvic trauma → suspect urethral injury. Do NOT catheterise blindly — perform a retrograde urethrogram first to avoid converting a partial tear into a complete transection.
1RETROGRADE URETHROGRAM — indication
Assessment of the urethra, most often the male anterior urethra. Two main referrals: trauma (pelvic fracture with posterior urethral injury; straddle/perineal injury with anterior bulbar injury) and strictures (site, length and calibre before urethroplasty or dilatation).
Blood at meatus + high-riding prostate + cannot void after pelvic fracture→Retrograde urethrogram BEFORE catheter
2RUG — technique & signs
Patient in a ~30° oblique position under fluoroscopy. A Foley catheter is seated in the fossa navicularis (balloon gently inflated with 1–2 mL) or a penile clamp is applied, and water-soluble contrast is injected retrogradely up the urethra while screening. Films are taken during injection to distend the urethra.
Contrast extravasation outside the urethral lumen → urethral disruption/rupture (partial if lumen still fills proximally, complete if no proximal filling).
Stricture → smooth or irregular narrowing; record site and length.
False passage → contrast tracking outside the normal channel, often iatrogenic from prior instrumentation.
3CYSTOGRAM — indication
Suspected bladder injury/rupture (classically pelvic fracture with frank haematuria), and also vesico-enteric or vesico-vaginal fistula and suspected post-operative bladder leak. The bladder must be adequately distended for the study to be reliable.
Pelvic fracture + gross haematuria→Cystogram to exclude bladder rupture
4CYSTOGRAM — technique & signs
Retrograde filling of the bladder via a urethral (or suprapubic) catheter with water-soluble contrast under gravity to full distension, screened with fluoroscopy. A post-drainage film is essential — a small extraperitoneal leak may only be seen once the bladder empties and residual contrast remains in the perivesical tissues.
Intraperitoneal rupture → contrast outlines bowel loops and tracks into the paracolic gutters/pouch of Douglas — needs surgical repair.
Extraperitoneal rupture → flame-shaped/feathery contrast in the perivesical and pelvic soft tissues — usually managed conservatively with catheter drainage.
💧Intraperitoneal bladder rupture
Contrast around bowel loops & paracolic gutters; dome tear; needs surgery.
🔥Extraperitoneal bladder rupture
Flame-shaped contrast in perivesical tissue; usually catheter drainage only.
🩸Anterior urethral injury
Bulbar urethra; straddle/perineal trauma; extravasation on RUG.
🦴Posterior urethral injury
Membranous/prostatic urethra; pelvic fracture; high-riding prostate.
🚩 Use water-soluble contrast only for both studies — never barium in the urinary tract, as extravasated barium into the peritoneum or soft tissues causes severe granulomatous reaction. Maintain strict asepsis (risk of introducing infection), watch for contrast reaction, minimise radiation, and obtain consent.
🎓 Sequence for lower urinary tract trauma: urethra before bladder. Do the retrograde urethrogram first; only once the urethra is shown to be intact (or a catheter is safely placed) do you proceed to the cystogram. The post-drainage film is what catches the subtle extraperitoneal leak.

A nephrostogram and an antegrade pyelogram are fluoroscopic contrast studies that opacify the pelvicalyceal system and ureter from above — contrast is injected antegradely down into the collecting system rather than retrogradely up from the bladder. They are the go-to studies when cystoscopic (retrograde) access has failed or is contraindicated, and when you need to define the level and cause of upper-tract obstruction, check a nephrostomy tube, or confirm a ureter is draining freely before removing a tube.

1DEFINITIONS & WHEN EACH IS USED

Antegrade pyelogram — water-soluble iodinated contrast injected antegradely into the pelvicalyceal system, either via a fresh percutaneous needle puncture of a calyx or through an existing nephrostomy tube, to opacify the collecting system and ureter from above. It answers the question: where and why is the upper tract obstructed?

Nephrostogram — contrast injected down an existing nephrostomy tube to check the tube's position, patency, and whether the ureter now drains freely to the bladder. Typically done before removing or capping a nephrostomy (once the cause of obstruction has been treated), or to confirm the position of a ureteric / antegrade stent.

Retrograde study failed or contraindicated→Opacify the system antegradely instead (antegrade pyelogram)
Obstruction treated, considering tube removal→Nephrostogram to confirm free drainage to bladder first
2INDICATIONS
Hydronephrosis / obstruction where the level or cause is unclear on other imaging
Failed retrograde study — cystoscopic ureteric cannulation unsuccessful or not possible
Assessment before nephrostomy removal — confirm the ureter drains freely to bladder
Antegrade ureteric stent insertion — roadmap and confirm stent position
Suspected leak / urinoma post-surgery (e.g. post-transplant, post-pyeloplasty) — look for contrast extravasation
3TECHNIQUE

Performed under fluoroscopy. For a fresh percutaneous puncture, ultrasound (and sometimes CT) guidance is used to direct the needle into a posterior calyx and avoid vessels and adjacent organs. Water-soluble iodinated contrast (never barium — this is not a bowel study) is injected via the nephrostomy tube or needle into the collecting system.

The operator screens the filling sequentially: calyces, then renal pelvis, then ureter, following contrast down to the bladder. Spot films are taken to document the level of any hold-up, drainage, and tube/stent position.

🚩 Inject gently and at low pressure. Over-distension of an infected, obstructed system forces bacteria and endotoxin into the circulation → pyelosepsis / urosepsis. Give antibiotic cover and decompress an infected obstructed kidney rather than over-filling it.
4WHAT YOU ASSESS
Level and cause of obstruction — where does contrast hold up, and why (stone, stricture, tumour, PUJ obstruction)?
Free drainage to bladder — does contrast pass down the ureter and empty into the bladder?
Contrast leak / urinoma — extravasation outside the collecting system
Tube / stent position — nephrostomy sited correctly, stent well positioned proximally and distally

The causes of upper-tract obstruction you are trying to distinguish:

🪨Stone
Filling defect / abrupt cut-off; calculus impacted in ureter or PUJ
🔻PUJ obstruction
Dilated pelvis with narrow pelviureteric junction; hold-up at the outlet of the pelvis
〰️Stricture
Smooth tapered narrowing; post-surgical, ischaemic, TB or radiation
🎯Tumour / extrinsic
Irregular intraluminal filling defect (urothelial tumour) or smooth extrinsic compression (nodes, mass)
🚩 Other risks: bleeding from the percutaneous puncture (vascular kidney — check clotting/platelets), contrast reaction, and ionising radiation. Obtain informed consent and use strict asepsis.
🎓 Remember the direction: antegrade = from above (down into the kidney), retrograde = from below (up from the bladder at cystoscopy). Reach for the antegrade route when the retrograde one has failed, and always confirm free drainage to the bladder on a nephrostogram before you pull a nephrostomy tube.

A sinogram or fistulogram is a simple fluoroscopic study in which water-soluble iodinated contrast is injected directly into an abnormal opening on the skin or into a tract, so its course can be mapped in real time. A sinus is a blind-ending, epithelialised tract that opens onto one surface only; a fistula is an abnormal tract connecting two epithelialised surfaces or organs (e.g. bowel to skin). The study answers one core clinical question: where does this tract go, and does it communicate with a viscus, cavity, or deep structure?

1Why you are doing it — indications

A sinogram/fistulogram is requested to define the anatomy of a persistent discharging opening and to identify any underlying communication that explains why it will not heal.

Non-healing wound or chronically discharging sinus→map tract length, depth and any deep source
Faeculent or high-output skin discharge post-op→suspected enterocutaneous fistula — confirm bowel communication
Recurrent perianal discharge / abscess→perianal fistula (though MRI is now preferred — see below)
Assessment of a chronic abscess cavity that will not resolve
Post-surgical wound breakdown / dehiscence with persistent tract
Suspected communication with bladder, joint or bone
2How it is performed — technique

The external opening is cleaned and, if needed, its margin marked. A fine catheter, cannula or small Foley catheter is gently inserted into the opening; a Foley balloon can be inflated to occlude the opening and prevent contrast leaking back out, improving tract filling.

Water-soluble iodinated contrast is injected under continuous fluoroscopy at low pressure, watching the tract fill in real time. Spot images are taken in more than one projection to demonstrate the tract's full course.

Length — how far the tract runs from the surface
Depth & direction — superficial vs deep, and where it heads
Branching — single blind tract vs complex/branching system
Communication — filling of bowel, bladder, a cavity, joint or bone
3What you assess — tract anatomy & communication

Interpretation moves from the surface inward: first the tract itself, then whether it ends blindly (sinus) or opens into a second structure (fistula).

Contrast pools in a blind cavity, no viscus fills→sinus / chronic abscess cavity
Contrast opacifies loops of bowel→enterocutaneous fistula — beware output & electrolyte loss
Tract reaches down to cortical bone / periosteum→concern for underlying osteomyelitis
4Underlying causes to consider

A tract that will not heal usually has a maintaining cause at its deep end. Naming it changes management far more than describing the tract alone.

🩸Crohn's disease
Transmural inflammation — classic cause of enterocutaneous and perianal fistulae
🧬Malignancy
Tumour eroding into skin/viscus — always consider in a persistent tract
🌀Diverticulitis
Colonic inflammation causing colovesical / colocutaneous fistulae
🪡Foreign body / suture
Retained material keeps a tract open until removed
🦠Tuberculosis
Chronic infective sinuses, especially with cold abscess or bony involvement
🦴Osteomyelitis
Deep bone infection sustaining a discharging sinus to the skin
🚩 Use water-soluble iodinated contrast, NEVER barium — barium that tracks into soft tissues or the peritoneal cavity is retained indefinitely, causing a granulomatous reaction and, in the peritoneum, severe barium peritonitis. Injecting into an infected cavity can force organisms into the bloodstream and precipitate sepsis, so inject gently at low pressure and stop if the patient becomes unwell.
🎓 For perianal fistula, MRI is the superior investigation — it shows the tract in relation to the anal sphincters and allows Parks classification (intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric) without radiation or catheterisation, so fluoroscopic fistulography is now largely reserved for cutaneous and post-surgical tracts. As always, gain informed consent and remember the study carries an ionising radiation dose.

Arthrography is the injection of contrast into a joint under fluoroscopic guidance to outline intra-articular structures — labrum, cartilage, capsule and rotator cuff. Although the classic conventional arthrogram (iodinated contrast alone) still exists, the modern mainstay is MR arthrography (or CT arthrography), where fluoroscopy is used simply to GUIDE accurate intra-articular needle placement before the joint is imaged in cross-section. It is the reference standard for subtle labral and rotator cuff tears.

1Indication — why arthrography
Evaluation of intra-articular structures that are poorly seen on plain imaging: labral tears (shoulder glenoid labrum, hip acetabular labrum), rotator cuff tears, the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) of the wrist, and articular cartilage. Distending the joint with contrast separates and outlines these structures so a tear can be shown. It also has therapeutic overlap — the same image-guided access is used to deliver intra-articular steroid and local anaesthetic.
Query shoulder labral / SLAP or rotator cuff tear→Fluoro-guided injection then MR arthrogram
2Technique — needle, test dose, injectate
Under aseptic technique and fluoroscopic guidance, a needle is advanced into the joint. Intra-articular position is confirmed with a small test injection of iodinated contrast — correct placement shows contrast flowing away from the needle tip along the joint recesses (not pooling in soft tissue). The therapeutic/diagnostic agent is then injected:
MR arthrogram — dilute gadolinium (typically ~1:200 in saline ± iodinated contrast ± local anaesthetic), then MRI.
CT arthrogram / conventional arthrogram — iodinated (water-soluble) contrast, then CT or fluoroscopic spot films.
The joint is distended to separate structures, then imaged promptly before contrast is absorbed or diluted.
3What you assess
The key sign of a tear is contrast tracking through a defect into or beyond a structure that should be intact.
Contrast smoothly outlining the labrum, cartilage and capsule — a clean interface is normal.
Contrast leaking into a labral tear (undercutting or filling the tear cleft) or through a rotator cuff tear into the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa.
Capsular abnormalities — a small, tight joint that resists distension and takes reduced volume suggests adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder).
4Key concepts — direct vs indirect
Direct arthrography = contrast injected straight into the joint (the fluoro-guided technique above) — gives best joint distension and is standard for labral/cuff work. Indirect arthrography = IV gadolinium that is absorbed into the joint over time; no injection needed but less distension and less specific. Remember the therapeutic overlap: the identical access route delivers steroid + local anaesthetic for symptomatic joints.
Best distension & sharpest labral detail needed→Direct (injected) MR arthrography
🦴Shoulder
Glenoid labrum (Bankart / SLAP tears), rotator cuff tears, adhesive capsulitis (reduced volume).
🦵Hip
Acetabular labral tears, FAI-related cartilage damage, loose bodies.
✋Wrist
TFCC tears; contrast leak between radiocarpal / midcarpal / distal radioulnar compartments = ligament tear.
🦿Knee / Elbow / Ankle
Cartilage defects, loose/osteochondral bodies, post-operative meniscal re-tear (CT/MR arthrogram).
🚩 Aseptic (sterile) technique is essential — introducing organisms into a joint causes septic arthritis. Watch for contrast reaction, and warn about post-procedure discomfort and transient swelling. Contraindications: overlying skin/soft-tissue infection (cellulitis) and significant bleeding risk / coagulopathy.
🎓 The test dose is the safety net: a small bolus of iodinated contrast that flows into the joint recesses confirms you are intra-articular BEFORE the expensive dilute-gadolinium injection — inject soft tissue and the MR arthrogram is wasted. Also counsel on radiation from fluoroscopy and take valid consent.

A T-tube (tube) cholangiogram is a fluoroscopic contrast study performed by injecting iodinated contrast directly into the biliary tree through an indwelling drain — most classically the T-shaped tube left in the common bile duct (CBD) after open exploration. Its central purpose is to confirm the ducts are clear of residual/retained stones and that contrast flows freely into the duodenum before the tube is removed.

1Indication & context

After biliary surgery — classically open CBD exploration for ductal stones — a latex/silastic T-tube is left in situ: the cross-bar sits within the CBD and the long limb drains bile externally. Before the tube is pulled, a cholangiogram is obtained (traditionally around day 7–10 post-op) to document a clear duct and free drainage.

T-tube cholangiogram — after open CBD exploration; the reference indication.
PTC-tube / percutaneous biliary drain check — contrast down an external/internal-external biliary drain to assess position, patency and drainage.
Other ‘tube cholangiograms’ — via any indwelling biliary drain to confirm the tree is clear before removal or exchange.
Day 7–10 post open CBD exploration→T-tube cholangiogram before tube removal
2Technique

Under strict asepsis, the tube is connected to a syringe of water-soluble iodinated contrast (never barium — barium in the biliary tree/peritoneum is inert but non-absorbable and disastrous if a leak is present). Contrast is injected gently, at low pressure, under continuous fluoroscopic screening.

Purge air bubbles from the tubing first — bubbles mimic filling defects (false-positive ‘stones’).
Screen the intra-hepatic and extra-hepatic ducts, then watch for free passage into the duodenum.
Take spot films; tilting/positioning helps fill the intra-hepatic radicals and avoid a dependent-duct false negative.
3What you assess
🪨Filling defect
Retained/residual CBD stone — a mobile, non-adherent radiolucent defect within the contrast column.
🩹Stricture
Focal narrowing / duct-calibre change — anastomotic or benign; assess upstream dilatation.
💧Bile leak
Extravasation of contrast outside the ducts — anastomotic or from the tube tract.
✅Free drainage
Unimpeded flow of contrast into the duodenum — the normal, reassuring end-point.
Clear duct + free flow to duodenum→Normal study — T-tube can be removed
4Result & safety

If the study is normal (clear tree, free duodenal flow), the T-tube is clamped and removed — the mature fibrous tract seals over. If a retained stone is found, the tube is left in situ and the stone dealt with, e.g. by ERCP or later percutaneous extraction via the mature T-tube tract (typically at ~6 weeks once the tract has matured).

🚩 Inject gently at low pressure. Over-pressurised injection into an obstructed or infected biliary system forces biliary-venous reflux of organisms into the bloodstream, precipitating cholangitis and Gram-negative septicaemia. Use strict asepsis and appropriate antibiotic cover; be alert to iodinated contrast reactions; and take informed consent.
🎓 An air bubble is the great mimic of a retained stone — both appear as radiolucent filling defects. Flushing air from the line before injection, and noting that bubbles are more rounded and rise while stones sit dependently, helps avoid a needless second procedure.

Every ward round runs on tubes and lines you can't see the tip of — a nasogastric tube for feeding, a PICC for chemotherapy, a nephrostomy draining an obstructed kidney. Confirming that each one sits where it should is bread-and-butter radiology, and getting it wrong can be fatal. Fluoroscopy and water-soluble contrast are the problem-solving tools you reach for when the bedside checks don't give a clean answer.

1NG / NJ tube — the two-check rule

A misplaced nasogastric tube feeding directly into the lung is a Never Event under NPSA guidance — it kills. Confirmation is therefore protocolised and does not rely on the old ‘whoosh test’ (auscultating injected air), which is unreliable and abandoned.

Check 1 — pH of aspirate. Aspirate gastric contents and test on CE-marked pH paper. A pH of ≤5.5 confirms a gastric (acidic) position and the tube can be used. This is the first-line and preferred check.
Check 2 — chest radiograph. Used when no aspirate is obtained, pH is >5.5, or the patient is on acid-suppression. The CXR is read by a competent, documented practitioner before feeding.
pH ≤5.5 on aspirate→Gastric — safe to feed, no CXR needed
No aspirate or pH >5.5→Get a CXR and read it before using the tube

Correct CXR position: the tube should descend in the midline following the oesophagus, bisect the carina, clearly not deviate into either bronchus, and its tip should lie below the left hemidiaphragm (i.e. in the stomach, ideally at least 10 cm beyond the gastro-oesophageal junction). A tube that veers laterally and follows a bronchial tree is in the lung — do not feed.

2When fluoroscopy takes over for NG/NJ placement

Bedside blind placement is standard. Fluoroscopic (screened) placement is reserved as a problem-solving tool for the difficult tube:

Repeatedly malpositioned or coiling tubes.
Post nasal / upper-airway / oesophageal surgery, or known strictures where a blind pass is hazardous.
Nasojejunal (NJ) tubes needing the tip carried past the pylorus into the jejunum, often placed under direct screening.

Under fluoroscopy the tube is advanced under live imaging and a small volume of water-soluble contrast (e.g. Gastrografin) can be injected to confirm the tip lies within the gastric or jejunal lumen before feeding is authorised. Water-soluble contrast is chosen deliberately — if the tube is actually in the airway or has perforated, spilled water-soluble agent is far safer than barium.

3PICC & central venous catheter tip check (the ‘linogram’)

The ideal tip of a PICC or central venous catheter sits at the cavoatrial junction or lower SVC — a high-flow position that minimises thrombosis and endothelial irritation. Tip position is confirmed on CXR; on a frontal film the cavoatrial junction is roughly two vertebral bodies below the carina.

When a line won't flush or won't aspirate, a linogram (contrast injection down the line under fluoroscopy) troubleshoots the problem:

Won't aspirate but flushes→Fibrin sheath or tip against vessel wall
Contrast tracks alongside the vein→Extravasation / catheter fracture — stop use
Contrast sleeves back over the tip on injection→Fibrin sheath — risk of drug tracking to skin

The linogram also demonstrates kinking, malposition (e.g. tip flipped up the internal jugular), and catheter patency. Use a small volume of water-soluble contrast with strict asepsis.

4The general principle of a tubogram

The same idea generalises to any indwelling tube: inject water-soluble contrast down it under fluoroscopy to confirm position, patency and track before it is relied upon. This is a ‘tubogram’ and the named study simply reflects the tube.

Nephrostogram — down a nephrostomy to check the tube sits in the collecting system, confirm drainage, and assess the level of any ureteric obstruction before antegrade stenting.
Tubogram / drain check — down a surgical or abscess drain to confirm the cavity, look for a residual collection or a communicating fistula/track.
Gastrostomy (PEG/RIG) contrast check — confirm the balloon/tip lies within the gastric lumen and there is no leak before feeding, especially in the early post-insertion period.

Always water-soluble, never barium, for these track/position checks — if the tube is misplaced or there is a leak, barium in the peritoneum, mediastinum or soft tissues causes a severe inflammatory reaction.

🍽️NG / NJ tube
Tip below left hemidiaphragm (NG) or past pylorus in jejunum (NJ). Confirm by pH ≤5.5 then CXR.
💉PICC
Peripherally inserted; tip at cavoatrial junction / lower SVC. Linogram if it won't flush or aspirate.
🩸Central line / Hickman
Tip at cavoatrial junction. Beware malposition up the IJ or across to the contralateral vein.
🫘Nephrostomy
Pigtail in the renal collecting system. Nephrostogram confirms position and obstruction level.
🥣Gastrostomy (PEG/RIG)
Tip/balloon in gastric lumen. Contrast check for leak before feeding early post-insertion.
🚰Surgical drain
Tubogram outlines the cavity/track and any residual collection or fistula.
🚩 Feeding through a misplaced NG tube sitting in the lung is a fatal Never Event. NEVER feed, flush or give medication down an NG tube until position is confirmed — pH ≤5.5 on aspirate, or a correctly interpreted CXR. The ‘whoosh’ auscultation test is unsafe and must not be used. Treat any uncertainty as a critical incident.
🚩 Other hazards: line-associated bloodstream infection (strict asepsis for any linogram/line handling), contrast reactions (ask about previous reactions and renal function), and ionising radiation from fluoroscopy (justify, minimise screening time, ALARP). Always use water-soluble contrast, not barium, for tube position and track checks.
🎓 Remember the NG mantra: pH first, film second, fluoroscopy for the difficult tube. Fluoroscopy and the contrast injection (linogram/tubogram) are problem-solving tools — you reach for them when the bedside checks fail or a line won't behave, not as the routine first-line confirmation.

Myelography (now almost always CT myelography) images the spinal canal, cord and nerve roots by opacifying the CSF within the thecal sac. Water-soluble non-ionic contrast is injected intrathecally by lumbar puncture under fluoroscopy, run up and down the thecal sac, and then usually followed by CT for cross-sectional detail. It has been largely replaced by MRI and is now reserved for patients who cannot have MRI or where MRI is equivocal.

1Why do it — and why so rarely now

Myelography assesses the spinal canal, cord and nerve roots. MRI has replaced it for almost all indications, so it is reserved for specific situations:

MRI contraindicated (pacemaker/certain implants)→CT myelography as the alternative
Severe claustrophobia or metal hardware causing MRI artefact→CT myelography visualises canal despite hardware
MRI equivocal / surgical planning needed→Define nerve-root compression, stenosis, disc, CSF leak, level of block

Used to demonstrate nerve-root compression, spinal (canal) stenosis, disc herniation, CSF leak, arachnoiditis, or to define a complete/partial block above and below for the surgeon.

2How it is performed

Image the brain first if raised intracranial pressure is suspected, obtain consent, then:

Lumbar puncture under fluoroscopic guidance, needle into the subarachnoid space.
Inject non-ionic, water-soluble, iodinated contrast that is specifically licensed for intrathecal use (a low-osmolar non-ionic agent, e.g. iohexol) into the thecal sac.
Tilt the table to run the contrast column up or down the thecal sac, screening the region of interest under fluoroscopy.
Proceed to CT (CT myelography) for cross-sectional detail of the canal, cord and roots.
🚩 NEVER-EVENT drug error: ONLY contrast specifically approved for intrathecal use (non-ionic, low-osmolar, e.g. iohexol) may be injected. Ionic contrast given intrathecally — classically gastrografin — is fatal: it causes severe neurotoxicity, intractable seizures and ascending myeloencephalopathy. Always confirm the agent and its intrathecal licence at the bedside before injecting.
3What you assess

Read the shape of the opacified contrast column within the thecal sac and its nerve-root sleeves:

Nerve-root sleeve filling defect or non-filling — a compressed or cut-off root.
Extradural indentation of the column — disc protrusion or osteophyte pressing in from outside the sac.
Complete or partial block — contrast stops abruptly; define the level above and below.
Cord compression — deformity/displacement of the cord silhouette.
CSF leak — contrast escaping outside the thecal sac.
4Key abnormalities to name
🦴Disc herniation
Extradural indentation of the contrast column with a filling defect / cut-off of the corresponding nerve-root sleeve.
⏳Spinal stenosis
Circumferential narrowing / waisting of the contrast column, sometimes a complete block; multilevel in degenerative canal stenosis.
🕸️Arachnoiditis
Clumped, matted or adherent nerve roots; irregular, loculated or absent root-sleeve filling within the sac.
💧CSF leak
Contrast tracking outside the thecal sac, localising the site of a dural tear or leak.
🎓 CT myelography earns its place precisely where MRI fails: it shows the bony canal and root sleeves in patients with spinal metalwork (which blooms and obscures MRI) or with MRI-incompatible implants. Think of it as the CSF-outlining problem-solver, not a first-line test.
🚩 Other risks & safeguards: post-LP (low-pressure) headache; LP is contraindicated in raised ICP / mass lesion due to risk of coning — image the brain first; infection (meningitis); bleeding; contrast reaction; and seizures — avoid drugs that lower the seizure threshold peri-procedure. Always consent for the LP and the intrathecal contrast.
